Bipolar disorder (BD)

No animal evidence was identified in the exact category.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

No animal evidence was identified in the exact category.

Summary of the Evidence

Four publications are listed in the exact Bipolar disorder category, with one additional 2025 analysis located by citation search. Together they represent five publications but four participant cohorts: a four-person case series, a five-person crossover study, a 15-person physiological study, and a 29-person open-label cohort reported again in a machine-learning analysis. Publication counts therefore exceed independent samples.

Human and clinical evidence

Mannu et al. described four people receiving PBM alongside lithium and reported patient-reported symptom changes; the uncontrolled case series cannot establish efficacy (2019). O’Donnell et al. studied five participants in a randomized sham-controlled crossover and reported improvements on selected cognitive tasks after five weekly sessions (2021). A later single-session study in 15 older adults measured cytochrome-c-oxidase and oxygenation changes; these are physiological outcomes, not mood improvement (O’Donnell et al. 2023). Barrett et al. treated 29 people with remitted bipolar disorder in an open-label study using six weekly sessions and reported cognitive improvement (2025). A 2025 machine-learning analysis of cognitive responses used the same 29-person cohort and is not an independent trial (Gonzalez-Lima et al. 2025). None of these reports establishes prevention of relapse or a mood-stabilizing effect.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo publication was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The records include 830-nm LED treatment as an adjunct to lithium and 1064-nm transcranial infrared laser stimulation. Treatment schedules range from one session to six weekly visits. The machine-learning article reuses data from the 29-person open-label cohort. Cognitive-task outcomes and physiological measures are distinct from mood episodes, remission durability, or relapse prevention.

Interpretation

The findings are exploratory and based on very small samples, open-label treatment, or physiological endpoints. Existing publications do not establish a clinical mood benefit, relapse prevention, or a role as a mood stabilizer.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for short-term cognitive or physiological outcomes No established evidence for mood stabilization or relapse prevention
Publications and records5 relevant publications: 4 exact-category titles plus 1 mapped 2025 analysis.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Evidence consists of small case, crossover, and exploratory studies. The 2021 sham-controlled crossover included five participants and found changes on selected cognitive tasks; the 2023 study measured physiological responses rather than clinical benefit. Two 2025 reports analyze the same 29-person cohort. No evidence establishes mood stabilization or relapse prevention.
